extracted.intended_audience: judges, juries, and patent litigators in U.S. federal patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions describing legal standards and element-by-element tests for patent claim construction, literal and indirect infringement theories (including means-plus-function, joint, induced, contributory, and §271(f)/(g) theories), and limits on the doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define boundaries; only claims can be infringed
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims are intended to define, in words, the boundaries of the inventor’s rights. Only the claims of the patent can be infringed. Neither the written description, nor the drawings of a patent can be infringed. Each of the claims must be considered individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must use the same claim meaning for both your decision on infringement and your decision on invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction by the Court
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the judge's job to provide to you the meaning of any claim language that must be interpreted. You must accept the meanings the judge gives you and use them when you decide whether any claim has been infringed and whether any claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [READ STIPULATIONS AND COURT’S CLAIM CONSTRUCTIONS]. Use these constructions when comparing accused product/method to the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claim interpretation (35 U.S.C. §112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee expresses an element as a 'means' or 'step' for performing a function, the clause is a means-plus-function element and requires special interpretation: it does not cover all means that perform the recited function; instead the claim covers the recited function and the structure/step described in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will determine the recited function and the structure/step described in the patent specification and drawings that perform the recited function; the jury must use that interpretation in deliberations. Give Instruction 2.2 only if the case involves means-plus-function claims; consider whether 2.2 is unnecessary when §112(f) governs but the phrase 'means for' or 'step for' is not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: General direct infringement comparison rule
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding infringement you may not compare the defendant’s accused product/method to the plaintiff’s commercial product/method. Rather, you must compare the defendant’s accused product/method to the claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent law gives the owner of a valid patent the right to exclude others from importing, making, using, offering to sell, or selling the claimed invention in the U.S. Practice note: distinguish direct vs indirect infringement, literal vs doctrine of equivalents, and induced vs contributory infringement to avoid jury confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—knowledge/intent immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: A party can directly infringe a patent without knowing of the patent or without knowing that what the party is doing is patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability for direct infringement under 35 U.S.C. §271(a) does not require proof of the defendant's knowledge or intent regarding the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct literal infringement—all claim elements required
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is literally infringed only if the defendant’s product/method includes each and every element/method step recited in that patent claim. If the defendant’s product/method does not contain one or more elements/method steps recited in a claim, the defendant does not literally infringe that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine literal infringement for each claim individually, using the court's constructions of claim terms. The same element of the accused product/method may satisfy more than one claim element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement—joint infringement (attribution of others' acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant did not perform each claimed method step or all acts to make/sell/import the accused product, the defendant may still directly infringe if the acts performed by others are attributable to the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution exists if (a) the defendant exercised direction or control over the other party when the other party performed the acts, or (b) the defendant and the other party formed a joint enterprise. A joint enterprise requires proof of (1) an agreement among members; (2) a common purpose; (3) a community of pecuniary interest; and (4) equal right to a voice in direction (equal control). If neither (a) nor (b) is found, no direct infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement of means-plus-function/step-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish infringement of a means-plus-function or step-plus-function claim, the plaintiff must prove that (1) the accused part/step performs the recited function, and (2) it is identical or equivalent to the structure/step described in the specification and drawings for performing that function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine whether the accused product/method has any structure/step performing the specific function. If not, the claim is not infringed. If yes, decide whether that structure/step is the same as or equivalent to the structure described in the specification. Equivalence is judged from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art: differences are equivalent if insubstantial (e.g., performs same function in substantially same way to achieve substantially same result). Both prongs must be met for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim (an independent claim) and includes all elements of the dependent claim plus all elements of the independent claim to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish literal infringement of a dependent claim, the plaintiff must prove the accused product/method includes each and every element of both the independent claim and the dependent claim. If the independent claim is not literally infringed, the dependent claim cannot be literally infringed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and effect of 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Comprising' means including the following but not excluding others. 'Consisting of' means including the following and excluding others. 'Consisting essentially of' means including the following and possibly unlisted components/steps that do not materially affect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim uses 'comprising', additional components do not avoid literal infringement if all claim elements are present. If a claim uses 'consisting of', presence of additional components means no literal infringement. If 'consisting essentially of', literal infringement exists if additional components do not negate an element or materially affect the basic and novel properties of the invention. Practice note: if the claim is literally infringed, no need to resort to doctrine of equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (DOE) test
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused product/method does not literally infringe, determine whether it infringes under the doctrine of equivalents: the product/method can infringe if it includes components/steps that are equivalent to those claim elements not literally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine each individual claim element and decide whether the accused product/method has an equivalent component/step for that element. An equivalent is insubstantially different—one way to show this is demonstrating it performs substantially the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result. Consider whether persons of ordinary skill at the time would have known of interchangeability; known interchangeability is not required. The same accused component may satisfy more than one element, and two accused components may satisfy a single claim element. If any claim element lacks an equivalent in the accused product/method, DOE infringement cannot be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on DOE—Prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee made a representation/argument or amended a claim for reasons related to patentability, there is a presumption that equivalent subject matter has been surrendered and DOE cannot be applied to those elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court determines whether prosecution history estoppel applies as a matter of law. If it applies, the court will instruct the jury which claim elements (by claim) cannot be the subject of DOE; those elements must be literally present for infringement. Remaining elements may be analyzed under DOE.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on DOE—Subject matter dedicated to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain subject matter from the patent has been dedicated to the public, the doctrine of equivalents cannot be applied to those elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will identify the elements to which DOE cannot be applied; each such element must be literally present in the accused product/method for infringement to be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active inducement of infringement (§271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: To find that the defendant actively induced another to directly infringe, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that (1) a single actor is responsible for direct infringement (all components/steps), and (2) the defendant actively induced those acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, the plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant aided, instructed, or otherwise acted with intent to cause acts by the alleged direct infringer that would constitute direct infringement; (2) the defendant knew of the patent or showed willful blindness to its existence; (3) the defendant knew or showed willful blindness that the actions of the alleged direct infringer would infringe at least one claim; and (4) the alleged direct infringer infringed at least one claim. Willful blindness requires (i) subjective belief of a high probability a patent existed covering the accused product/method, and (ii) deliberate actions to avoid learning of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by supply of components abroad—§271(f)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(1), plaintiff must prove: (1) the product as intended to be assembled outside the U.S. included all elements of at least one claim; (2) the defendant supplied (or caused to be supplied) components from the U.S. that made up all or a substantial portion of the invention of a claim; and (3) the defendant specifically intended to induce the combination of the components into a product that would infringe if assembled in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'substantial portion' requires a quantitative, not qualitative, assessment—export of a single component of a multi-component invention cannot create liability under §271(f)(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement (§271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish contributory infringement, the plaintiff must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that: (1) someone other than the defendant has directly infringed a claimed invention; (2) the defendant sold, offered for sale, or imported within the U.S. a component of the infringing product or an apparatus for use in the infringing method; (3) the component/apparatus is not a staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use; (4) the component/apparatus constitutes a material part of the claimed invention; and (5) the defendant knew that the component was especially made or adapted for use in an infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'staple article or commodity of commerce capable of substantial non-infringing use' has other non-incidental uses that are not occasional, farfetched, impractical, experimental, or hypothetical. Defendant's knowledge may be shown by willful blindness (subjective high probability and deliberate avoidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by supply of specially made components abroad—§271(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(f)(2), plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant actually supplied components from the U.S. into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) the defendant knew or should have known the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) the defendant intended for the components to be combined into that product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, as long as the defendant intended the components to be combined into a product that would have infringed a claim if combined in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import/sale/use of product made by patented process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: To show infringement under §271(g), plaintiff must prove: (1) the defendant imported, sold, offered for sale, or used a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim; (2) the product was made between the patent issue date and the patent expiration (or date of trial); and (3) the defendant imported/sold/offered/used the product between the patent issue date and the patent expiration (or date of trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the evidence establishes that the product was 'made by' the claimed process. If the product was materially changed by later processes, or the product is only a trivial or non-essential part of another product, then the product was not 'made by' the claimed process and §271(g) liability does not apply.
